key_insight: Vision-language models increasingly ignore visual evidence and conform to overstated textual prompts as object counts grow; this prompt-induced hallucination is driven by strong language priors and weak visual integration.
problem_solved: Explains why and how VLMs hallucinate when prompts assert facts about images (e.g., overstating object counts), isolating the mechanisms that make models favor text over vision in a controlled object-counting setting.
method: Construct a controlled object-counting benchmark where prompts intentionally overstate the number of objects and measure model responses across differing true counts.
Quantify hallucination rates as a function of object count and compare correction vs conformity behavior.
Perform diagnostic analyses (e.g., attention/representation probing and ablations) to identify reliance on language priors and failures in visual grounding.
impact: Provides actionable understanding for ML practitioners to detect, evaluate, and mitigate prompt-induced hallucinations in VLMs—guiding better prompt design, training strategies, and auditing practices.
visual_elements: Line or bar chart: hallucination rate (y) vs true object count (x) showing rising conformity with higher counts.
Side-by-side example panel: image + overstating prompt + model answer (correct vs hallucinated) to illustrate behavior.
Schematic diagram: information flow showing relative weighting of prompt (language prior) vs visual evidence (grounding).
Attention/ablation heatmap: visualization showing reduced visual feature influence or shifted attention when hallucination occurs.
paper_title: Mechanisms of Prompt-Induced Hallucination in Vision-Language Models
paper_authors: William Rudman, Michal Golovanevsky, Dana Arad, Yonatan Belinkov, Ritambhara Singh
